glossary.definition: For a set \(S\), the Cartesian product \(S \times S\) is the set of all ordered pairs \((a, b)\) where \(a \in S\) and \(b \in S\). In an ordered pair, the order of the two elements matters.
A binary operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is a rule (function) that assigns to each ordered pair \((a, b) \in S \times S\) a single element \(a * b\) in \(S\).
A subset \(H\) of a set \(S\) is closed under a binary operation \(*\) if combining any two elements \(a, b \in H\) always gives an element \(a * b\) that is still inside \(H\).
When a subset \(H \subseteq S\) is closed under \(*\), the induced operation on \(H\) is the binary operation obtained by restricting \(*\) to pairs of elements from \(H\).
A binary operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is commutative if \(a * b = b * a\) for all \(a, b \in S\). Swapping the order of the two elements does not change the result.
A binary operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is associative if \((a * b) * c = a * (b * c)\) for all \(a, b, c \in S\). Regrouping parentheses does not change the result.
An element \(e\) in a set \(S\) with binary operation \(*\) is an identity element if \(a * e = e * a = a\) for every \(a \in S\). Combining any element with \(e\) leaves that element unchanged.

In a set \(S\) with operation \(*\) and identity \(e\), an inverse of \(x\in S\) is \(y\in S\) with \(x*y=y*x=e\). Existence and uniqueness are guaranteed in a group, but not in an arbitrary binary structure.
A square grid that defines a binary operation on a finite set by placing the product \(a * b\) in the row labeled \(a\) on the left and the column labeled \(b\) at the top.
A set \(S\) together with a binary operation \(*\) defined on \(S\), written \(\langle S, * \rangle\).
A rule \(*\) on a set \(S\) is everywhere defined if it assigns an answer to every possible ordered pair \((a, b) \in S \times S\), with no missing pairs.
A rule \(*\) on a set \(S\) is well defined if it assigns only one unambiguous answer to each ordered pair \((a, b) \in S \times S\).
An element \(x\) in a set \(S\) with binary operation \(*\) is idempotent if \(x * x = x\). Combining the element with itself gives the same element back.

A group \(\langle G, * \rangle\) is a set \(G\) closed under a binary operation \(*\) such that \(*\) is associative (\(\mathscr{G}_1\)), \(G\) has an identity element \(e\) (\(\mathscr{G}_2\)), and every element \(a \in G\) has an inverse \(a' \in G\) (\(\mathscr{G}_3\)).
A group \(\langle G, * \rangle\) whose binary operation \(*\) is commutative, meaning \(a * b = b * a\) for all \(a, b \in G\).
A one-to-one function from the plane onto itself that preserves the distance between any two points, such as a rotation, translation, or reflection.
The group \(GL(n, \mathbb{R})\) consisting of all invertible \(n \times n\) matrices with real entries under matrix multiplication.
A set \(S\) together with an associative binary operation \(*\). Every group is a semigroup, but a semigroup need not have an identity or inverses.
A semigroup \(\langle S, * \rangle\) that has an identity element \(e\) for the binary operation \(*\).

A one-to-one and onto function \(f : G_1 \to G_2\) between two groups \(\langle G_1, *_1 \rangle\) and \(\langle G_2, *_2 \rangle\) that satisfies \(f(a *_1 b) = f(a) *_2 f(b)\) for all \(a, b \in G_1\).
For a map \(f : G_1 \to G_2\) between two binary structures, the condition \(f(a *_1 b) = f(a) *_2 f(b)\) for all \(a, b \in G_1\), meaning the operations match after relabeling.
A subset H of a group G is a subgroup if H is closed under the group operation of G and forms a group under the induced operation.
A subgroup H of a group G is proper if H is strictly contained in G (H ≠ G).
The subgroup of a group G consisting solely of the identity element {e}.
The operation on a closed subset \(H\) obtained by applying exactly the original rule from \(G\) to inputs in \(H\). Closure is needed so all outputs stay in \(H\).
The subgroup ⟨a⟩ = {aⁿ | n ∈ ℤ} consisting of all integer powers (or integer multiples in additive notation) of an element a.
A group G is cyclic if there exists an element a in G such that G = ⟨a⟩.
An element a of a group G that generates the whole group, meaning ⟨a⟩ = G.
The order |a| of an element a in a group G is the cardinality |⟨a⟩| of its cyclic subgroup, which equals the smallest positive integer m such that aᵐ = e when finite.
aliases: order of an element in a group

glossary.definition: For a positive integer r and non-negative integer s, the positive generator d of the cyclic subgroup {nr + ms | n, m ∈ ℤ} under addition.
The theorem that the greatest common divisor d = gcd(r, s) can always be expressed as an integer linear combination d = nr + ms for some n, m ∈ ℤ.
Two integers r and s are relatively prime if gcd(r, s) = 1.
A mapping φ: G → G' between two groups such that φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b) for all a, b ∈ G.
The kernel of a homomorphism φ: G → G', denoted Ker(φ), is the subgroup {x ∈ G | φ(x) = e'} consisting of all elements in G mapped to the identity in G'.
The injective homomorphism φ: G → S_G given by φ(x) = λ_x, where λ_x(g) = xg for all g ∈ G.
aliases: left regular representation of a group

glossary.definition: The theorem stating that every group is isomorphic to a group of permutations.
A cycle of length 2 in a symmetric group, interchanging two distinct elements and fixing all others.
For any nonempty set \(A\), the collection \(S_A\) of all one-to-one maps from \(A\) onto \(A\) forms a group under function composition.
glossary.example: In \(S_A\), the identity map \(\iota(a) = a\) is the identity element and the inverse function \(\sigma^{-1}\) is the group inverse.

glossary.definition: The group \(S_n\) of all permutations of the finite set \(\{1, 2, \dots, n\}\) under function composition, having order \(n!\).
glossary.example: The group \(S_3\) has \(3! = 6\) elements and is the smallest nonabelian group.

glossary.definition: A permutation \((a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k)\) that sends \(a_1 \mapsto a_2 \mapsto \dots \mapsto a_k \mapsto a_1\) in a loop and leaves all other elements fixed.
glossary.example: In \(S_6\), the 3-cycle \((1, 3, 6)\) sends \(1 \mapsto 3\), \(3 \mapsto 6\), \(6 \mapsto 1\), and fixes \(2, 4, 5\).

glossary.definition: A 2-cycle \((a, b)\) that swaps two distinct elements \(a\) and \(b\) while leaving every other element fixed.
glossary.example: In \(S_n\) for \(n \ge 2\), the transposition \((1, 2)\) is its own inverse since \((1, 2)(1, 2) = \iota\).

glossary.definition: A collection of cycles in which no element appears in more than one cycle; disjoint cycles always commute with each other.
For a permutation \(\sigma \in S_A\) and \(a \in A\), the orbit of \(a\) is the set \(\{\sigma^k(a) \mid k \in \mathbb{Z}\}\) of all elements reached by applying powers of \(\sigma\) to \(a\).
A permutation of a finite set that can be expressed as a product of an even number of transpositions.
glossary.example: The identity \(\iota = (1, 2)(1, 2)\) and any 3-cycle \((a, b, c) = (a, c)(a, b)\) are even permutations.

glossary.definition: A permutation of a finite set that can be expressed as a product of an odd number of transpositions.
glossary.example: Every single transposition \((a, b)\) and every 4-cycle \((a, b, c, d) = (a, d)(a, c)(a, b)\) is an odd permutation.

glossary.definition: The group homomorphism \(\operatorname{sgn}: S_n \to \{1, -1\}\) defined by \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = 1\) if \(\sigma\) is even and \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = -1\) if \(\sigma\) is odd.
glossary.example: Since \(1\) is the multiplicative identity of \(\{1, -1\}\), the kernel \(\operatorname{Ker}(\operatorname{sgn})\) is the alternating group \(A_n\).

glossary.definition: The subgroup \(A_n\) of \(S_n\) consisting of all even permutations of \(\{1, 2, \dots, n\}\); for \(n \ge 2\), its order is \(n!/2\).
glossary.example: In \(S_3\), the alternating group is \(A_3 = \{\iota, (1, 2, 3), (1, 3, 2)\}\) of order \(6/2 = 3\).

glossary.definition: For a subgroup \(H\) of a group \(G\), the equivalence relation \(\sim_L\) on \(G\) defined by \(a \sim_L b\) if and only if \(a^{-1}b \in H\).
glossary.example: The equivalence classes of \(\sim_L\) partition \(G\) into the left cosets \(aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}\).

glossary.definition: For a subgroup \(H\) of a group \(G\) and an element \(a \in G\), the subset \(aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}\) (written \(a + H\) in additive notation).
glossary.example: In \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\) with \(H = \langle 3 \rangle = \{0, 3, 6, 9\}\), the left coset containing \(1\) is \(1 + H = \{1, 4, 7, 10\}\).

glossary.definition: If \(H\) is a subgroup of a finite group \(G\), then the order of \(H\) is a divisor of the order of \(G\).
glossary.example: A group of order \(12\) can only have subgroups of orders \(1, 2, 3, 4, 6,\) or \(12\).

glossary.definition: For a subgroup \(H\) of a group \(G\), the index \((G:H)\) is the number of distinct left cosets of \(H\) in \(G\).
glossary.example: When \(G\) is finite, \((G:H) = |G|/|H|\); for instance, \((S_n : A_n) = 2\) for \(n > 1\).

glossary.definition: For a subgroup \(H\) of a group \(G\) and \(a \in G\), the subset \(Ha = \{ha \mid h \in H\}\), which is the equivalence class of \(a\) under \(a \sim_R b \iff ab^{-1} \in H\).
glossary.example: In \(D_4\) with \(H = \{\iota, \mu\}\), the right coset \(H\rho = \{\rho, \mu\rho\}\) differs from the left coset \(\rho H = \{\rho, \mu\rho^3\}\).

glossary.definition: For a group homomorphism \(\phi: G \to G'\), the kernel \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \{g \in G \mid \phi(g) = e'\}\) is the subgroup of elements in \(G\) mapped to the identity \(e'\) of \(G'\).
glossary.example: For \(\det: GL(2, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}^*\), \(\operatorname{Ker}(\det)\) is the subgroup of \(2 \times 2\) matrices with determinant \(1\).

glossary.definition: If \(\phi : G \to G'\) is a group homomorphism with kernel \(K\) and \(\gamma_K : G \to G/K\) is the canonical homomorphism, there is a unique isomorphism \(\mu : G/K \to \phi[G]\) such that \(\phi(x) = \mu(\gamma_K(x))\) for all \(x \in G\).
glossary.example: For \(\phi : \mathbb{Z}_{12} \to \mathbb{Z}_3\) with \(\phi(1) = 2\), the kernel is \(K = \{0, 3, 6, 9\}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}/K \simeq \mathbb{Z}_3\).

glossary.definition: For a normal subgroup \(N\) of a group \(G\), the natural map \(\gamma : G \to G/N\) defined by \(\gamma(x) = xN\) that sends each element to its coset.
glossary.example: In \(\mathbb{Z}_8\) with \(K = \{0, 4\}\), the canonical homomorphism sends \(1 \mapsto \{1, 5\}\).

glossary.definition: For subgroups \(H\) and \(N\) of a group \(G\), the set \(HN = \{hn \mid h \in H, n \in N\}\) of all products of an element of \(H\) with an element of \(N\).
glossary.example: In an additive group \(\mathbb{Z}\), the product of \(N = \langle n \rangle\) and \(H = \langle h \rangle\) is written \(N + H = \langle \gcd(n, h) \rangle\).

glossary.definition: The join \(H \vee N\) of subgroups \(H\) and \(N\) of \(G\) is the intersection of all subgroups of \(G\) containing \(HN\), which is the smallest subgroup containing both \(H\) and \(N\).
glossary.example: When \(N\) is a normal subgroup of \(G\), Lemma 16.4 shows that \(H \vee N = HN = NH\).

glossary.definition: If \(H\) is a subgroup of a group \(G\) and \(N\) is a normal subgroup of \(G\), then \((HN)/N \simeq H/(H \cap N)\).
glossary.example: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), for \(N = \langle n \rangle\) and \(H = \langle h \rangle\), \((N + H)/N = \langle \gcd(n, h) \rangle / \langle n \rangle \simeq \langle h \rangle / \langle \operatorname{lcm}(n, h) \rangle\).

glossary.definition: If \(H\) and \(K\) are normal subgroups of a group \(G\) with \(K \le H\), then \(H/K\) is a normal subgroup of \(G/K\) and \(G/H \simeq (G/K)/(H/K)\).
glossary.example: In \(G = \mathbb{Z}_8\) with \(H = \langle 2 \rangle\) and \(K = \langle 4 \rangle\), \((\mathbb{Z}_8/\langle 4 \rangle)/(\langle 2 \rangle/\langle 4 \rangle) \simeq \mathbb{Z}_8/\langle 2 \rangle\).

glossary.definition: A set \(R\) with two binary operations \(+\) (addition) and \(\cdot\) (multiplication) such that \(\langle R, + \rangle\) is an abelian group, multiplication is associative, and the left and right distributive laws hold.
glossary.example: The integers \(\langle \mathbb{Z}, +, \cdot \rangle\), modulo integers \(\mathbb{Z}_n\), and matrix rings \(M_n(\mathbb{R})\) are rings.

glossary.definition: The ring axioms stating that for all \(a, b, c \in R\), left distribution \(a \cdot (b + c) = (a \cdot b) + (a \cdot c)\) and right distribution \((a + b) \cdot c = (a \cdot c) + (b \cdot c)\) hold.
glossary.example: The distributive laws link addition and multiplication and are used to prove \(0a = 0\) in Theorem 22.8.

glossary.definition: A map \(\phi : R \to R'\) between rings such that \(\phi(a + b) = \phi(a) + \phi(b)\) and \(\phi(ab) = \phi(a)\phi(b)\) for all \(a, b \in R\).
glossary.example: The reduction map \(\phi : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_n\) sending \(a\) to its remainder modulo \(n\) is a ring homomorphism.

glossary.definition: For a ring homomorphism \(\phi : R \to R'\), the set \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \{a \in R \mid \phi(a) = 0'\}\) of elements mapped to the additive identity \(0'\) of \(R'\).
glossary.example: A ring homomorphism \(\phi\) is one-to-one if and only if \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \{0\}\).

glossary.definition: For the ring \(F\) of functions \(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) and a fixed \(a \in \mathbb{R}\), the ring homomorphism \(\phi_a : F \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(\phi_a(f) = f(a)\).
glossary.example: Finding a real root \(a\) of a polynomial \(p(x) = 0\) means finding \(a \in \mathbb{R}\) with \(\phi_a(p) = 0\).

glossary.definition: A ring homomorphism \(\phi : R \to R'\) that is both one-to-one and onto \(R'\); the rings \(R\) and \(R'\) are then called isomorphic.
glossary.example: When \(\gcd(r, s) = 1\), the rings \(\mathbb{Z}_{rs}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_r \times \mathbb{Z}_s\) are isomorphic.

glossary.definition: A ring \(R\) in which multiplication is commutative, meaning \(ab = ba\) for all \(a, b \in R\).
glossary.example: The ring \(\mathbb{Z}\) is commutative, whereas the matrix ring \(M_n(\mathbb{R})\) for \(n \ge 2\) is not commutative.

glossary.definition: A multiplicative identity element \(1\) in a ring \(R\) such that \(1a = a1 = a\) for all \(a \in R\); a ring possessing \(1\) is called a ring with unity.
glossary.example: The ring \(\mathbb{Z}\) has unity \(1\), whereas the ring \(2\mathbb{Z}\) of even integers has no unity.

glossary.definition: The one-element ring \(\{0\}\) with \(0 + 0 = 0\) and \((0)(0) = 0\), which is the only ring in which \(0\) also serves as a multiplicative identity.
glossary.example: In any ring with more than one element, \(0a = 0\) prevents \(0\) from being a multiplicative identity.

glossary.definition: An element \(u\) in a ring \(R\) with unity \(1 \ne 0\) that has a multiplicative inverse \(u^{-1} \in R\) satisfying \(uu^{-1} = u^{-1}u = 1\).
glossary.example: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), the only units are \(1\) and \(-1\); in \(\mathbb{Z}_{14}\), the units are \(1, 3, 5, 9, 11, 13\).

glossary.definition: A ring \(R\) with unity \(1 \ne 0\) in which every nonzero element is a unit (has a multiplicative inverse in \(R\)). Also called a skew field.
glossary.example: A noncommutative division ring is called a strictly skew field, while a commutative division ring is a field.

glossary.definition: A commutative division ring, that is, a commutative ring with unity \(1 \ne 0\) in which every nonzero element is a unit.
glossary.example: The rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\), real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\), complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\), and \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) for prime \(p\) are fields.

glossary.definition: A subset \(S\) of a ring \(R\) that is itself a ring under the induced addition and multiplication from \(R\).
glossary.example: By Exercise 50 (Section 22), \(S \subseteq R\) is a subring iff \(0 \in S\), \(a - b \in S\), and \(ab \in S\) for all \(a, b \in S\).

glossary.definition: A subset \(K\) of a field \(F\) that forms a field under the operations of addition and multiplication induced from \(F\).
glossary.example: The field \(\mathbb{Q}\) of rational numbers is a subfield of the field \(\mathbb{R}\) of real numbers.

glossary.definition: A nonzero element participating in \(ab=0\) with another nonzero element. In a commutative ring a zero divisor \(a\ne0\) has some \(b\ne0\) with \(ab=0\). Zero itself is excluded; in noncommutative rings either left or right zero divisors may occur.
glossary.example: In \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\), \(3\) and \(4\) are divisors of 0 because \(3 \ne 0\), \(4 \ne 0\), and \((3)(4) = 0\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\).

glossary.definition: The multiplicative property in a ring \(R\) stating that \(ab = ac\) with \(a \ne 0\) implies \(b = c\), and \(ba = ca\) with \(a \ne 0\) implies \(b = c\).
glossary.example: By Theorem 23.6, the cancellation laws hold in a ring \(R\) if and only if \(R\) has no divisors of 0.

glossary.definition: A commutative ring \(D\) with unity \(1 \ne 0\) that contains no divisors of 0.
glossary.example: The ring \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) for any prime \(p\) are integral domains, whereas \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\) is not.

glossary.definition: The least positive integer \(n\) such that \(n \cdot a = 0\) for all \(a \in R\); if no such positive integer exists, the ring \(R\) has characteristic 0.
glossary.example: The ring \(\mathbb{Z}_n\) has characteristic \(n\), whereas \(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{R}\), and \(\mathbb{C}\) have characteristic 0.

glossary.definition: A function that is both one-to-one (equal outputs require equal inputs) and onto (every target element is an output).
A bijection \(f:S\to T\) between binary structures with \(f(a*b)=f(a)\circ f(b)\) for all \(a,b\in S\). It preserves the operation; group axioms are not required.
The cardinality \(|G|\) of the underlying set of a group. For a finite group this is the number of elements, including the identity.
A bijection from a set onto itself. Its inverse reverses the map, and its product with another permutation is function composition, from right to left in this deck.
A subgroup \(N\le G\) with \(gN=Ng\) for every \(g\in G\), equivalently \(gng^{-1}\in N\) for every \(g\in G,n\in N\). Kernels are normal.

For a normal subgroup \(N\trianglelefteq G\), the group \(G/N\) whose elements are cosets \(gN\), with \((aN)(bN)=(ab)N\). The identity is the coset \(N\). Normality makes the operation independent of representatives.
Integers \(a,b\) are congruent modulo \(n\ge1\) if \(n\) divides \(a-b\). In \(\mathbb Z_n\) one records only remainders \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\); sums and products are reduced to those remainders.

cards.label: Definitions 1.1 & 1.4
cards.title: What is a Binary Operation and a Closed Subset?
cards.body: A binary operation is a rule that takes two elements of a set \(S\), in a specified order, and returns exactly one element of \(S\). Formally, \(*:S\times S\to S\), with output written \(a*b\). Every ordered pair must have an output. A subset \(H\subseteq S\) is closed if \(a*b\in H\) whenever \(a,b\in H\). Only then does the same rule give an induced operation on \(H\).
examples: Even integers are closed under addition; odd integers are not.

cards.label: Definitions 1.11 & 1.12
cards.title: What are Commutative and Associative Operations?
cards.body: Commutativity means that swapping the two inputs never changes the output: \(a*b=b*a\) for all \(a,b\in S\). Associativity means that changing brackets never changes the output: \((a*b)*c=a*(b*c)\) for all \(a,b,c\in S\). Associativity preserves the order of the inputs. One example that agrees cannot prove either law; one disagreement disproves it.
examples: Addition is both; subtraction is neither.
Function composition is associative but usually not commutative.

Choose the \(n\) diagonal cells and the \(n(n-1)/2\) cells above them freely: there are \(n^{n(n+1)/2}\) choices. For two elements the counts are \(16\) and \(8\). cards.label: Exercises 43 (Section 1) and 31 (Section 2)
cards.title: What is an Idempotent Element?
cards.body: An element \(a\) is idempotent if combining it with itself returns \(a\): \(a*a=a\). For example, every input is idempotent under minimum, since \(\min(a,a)=a\). If the operation is associative and commutative and \(a,b\) are idempotent, regrouping and reordering gives \((a*b)*(a*b)=(a*a)*(b*b)=a*b\); thus their product is idempotent too.
examples: In a group, \(a*a=a*e\) implies \(a=e\) by cancellation.

cards.title: How to prove two structures are not isomorphic
cards.body: Isomorphisms preserve commutativity, associativity, identities, and inverse equations. For example, if \(S\) is commutative and \(u=f(a),v=f(b)\) are arbitrary elements of \(T\), then \(u\circ v=f(a*b)=f(b*a)=v\circ u\). Onto is what lets us represent every \(u,v\) this way. Thus a commutative structure cannot be isomorphic to a noncommutative one. Different cardinalities also rule out a bijection. One failed candidate map does not prove that no isomorphism exists. Isomorphism is an equivalence relation: the identity map preserves the operation; inverse bijections preserve it by applying \(f^{-1}\) to \(f(a*b)=f(a)\circ f(b)\); and composing two operation-preserving bijections again preserves the operation. Thus one can work in either direction, and a chain of isomorphisms preserves structure.

cards.body: In a finite group, each row and column contains each element exactly once, because each equation \(ax=b\) or \(ya=b\) has a unique solution. For order 2, the last table cell must be \(a^2=e\). For order 3, label the nonidentity elements \(a,b\). The value \(a^2\) cannot be \(a\) by cancellation, or \(e\) since the rest of row \(a\) would force \(ab=b=eb\), again contradicting cancellation. Thus \(a^2=b\), and the remaining entries are forced. These tables are realized by \(\mathbb Z_2\) and \(\mathbb Z_3\), so associativity is justified. Up to isomorphism there is one group of each order 1, 2 and 3. At order 4 there are two: cyclic \(\mathbb Z_4\), with an element of order 4, and the Klein four-group, in which every nonidentity element has order 2. Both are abelian. A table with each element once in every row and column need not be associative, so this condition alone is insufficient.

cards.title: What is a subgroup?
cards.body: A subgroup \(H\le G\) is a subset that is itself a group using exactly the operation inherited from \(G\). It must contain the same identity and the inverse of each of its elements. cards.title: What is a cyclic subgroup?
cards.body: The cyclic subgroup generated by \(a\) contains all integer powers: \(\langle a\rangle=\{a^n:n\in\mathbb Z\}\). Include \(a^0=e\) and negative powers \(a^{-n}=(a^{-1})^n\). Products and inverses stay in this set because exponents add and negate. Every subgroup containing \(a\) must contain these elements, so it is the smallest one. If it equals \(G\), then \(G\) is cyclic and \(a\) is a generator. For additive groups replace powers \(a^n\) by integer multiples \(na\).

cards.title: What is the order of an element?
cards.body: The order \(\operatorname{ord}(a)\) counts the distinct elements of \(\langle a\rangle\). If finite, it is the least positive integer \(m\) with \(a^m=e\); the powers are \(e,a,\ldots,a^{m-1}\). If no positive power returns to \(e\), the order is infinite. This is different from the order \(|G|\) of a group, which counts all its elements. In an additive group the condition is \(ma=0\).
examples: In \((\mathbb Z,+)\), no positive multiple of \(1\) is \(0\), so its order is infinite.

cards.title: Cyclic groups are abelian (Theorem 6.1)
cards.body: Every cyclic group \(G = \langle a \rangle\) is abelian because powers of the generator commute: \(a^r a^s = a^{r+s} = a^{s+r} = a^s a^r\).

cards.title: Subgroups of cyclic groups (Theorem 6.6)
cards.body: The division algorithm says: for any integer \(n\) and positive integer \(m\), there are unique integers \(q,r\) such that \(n=mq+r\) and \(0\le r<m\). It is the key to proving every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic: choose the smallest positive exponent \(m\) whose power lies in the subgroup, then show every allowed exponent is a multiple of \(m\). For \((\mathbb Z,+)\), the subgroups are exactly \(n\mathbb Z\), with \(n\ge0\); \(0\mathbb Z=\{0\}\).

cards.title: What is the greatest common divisor?
cards.body: For integers \(r>0\) and \(s\ge0\), the greatest common divisor \(d=\gcd(r,s)\) is the largest positive integer dividing both. The set of all integer linear combinations \(\{ur+vs:u,v\in\mathbb Z\}\) is the subgroup \(d\mathbb Z\). Thus \(d=ur+vs\) for some integers \(u,v\): this is Bézout’s identity. Integers are relatively prime when their gcd is \(1\).

cards.title: Classification of cyclic groups (Theorem 6.10)
cards.body: Every infinite cyclic group is isomorphic to \(\langle \mathbb{Z}, + \rangle\). Every finite cyclic group of order \(n\) is isomorphic to \(\langle \mathbb{Z}_n, +_n \rangle\).

cards.label: Theorem 4.8
cards.title: What is the permutation group \(S_A\)?
cards.body: A permutation of \(A\) is a bijection from \(A\) to itself. The set \(S_A\) of all such maps forms a group under composition: \((\sigma\mu)(a)=\sigma(\mu(a))\), so apply \(\mu\) first. A composite of bijections is a bijection, giving closure; composition is associative. The identity is \(\iota(a)=a\), and the inverse bijection undoes each map in both orders.
examples: Throughout this deck, compose from right to left.

cards.label: Definition 4.9
cards.title: What is the symmetric group \(S_n\)?
cards.body: The symmetric group \(S_n\) contains all permutations of \(\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\). To build one, choose the image of 1 in \(n\) ways, then the image of 2 in \(n-1\) ways, and continue without repeating outputs. There are \(n!\) permutations. The group depends on the number of labels rather than their names.

cards.label: Orbits
cards.title: What is the orbit of an element under a permutation?
cards.body: For a permutation \(\sigma\), start at \(a\) and repeatedly apply \(\sigma\) or its inverse. All points reached form the orbit \(\{\sigma^k(a):k\in\mathbb Z\}\); \(k=0\) includes \(a\) itself. In a finite set, these are precisely the entries of the disjoint cycle containing \(a\). Orbits are equal or disjoint and together cover the set; count fixed points as singleton orbits.

cards.label: Examples 8.17–8.18
cards.title: Transposition Products and Orbits (Examples 8.17–8.18)
cards.body: Every permutation in \(S_n\) (\(n \ge 2\)) is a product of transpositions (Example 8.17). In Example 8.18, \(\sigma = (1, 2, 6)(3, 5)(4) \in S_6\) has three orbits: \(\{1, 2, 6\}\), \(\{3, 5\}\), and \(\{4\}\), while \(\iota \in S_n\) has \(n\) singleton orbits.

cards.label: Theorem 8.19
cards.title: Invariance of Parity (Theorem 8.19)
cards.body: Theorem 8.19: No permutation in \(S_n\) can be expressed both as a product of an even number of transpositions and as a product of an odd number of transpositions.

cards.label: Proof · 8.19
cards.title: Orbit-Counting Proof (Theorem 8.19 & Exercise 42)
cards.body: Left multiplication by a transposition \(\tau=(i,j)\) swaps the two arrows whose outputs were \(i\) and \(j\). If these arrows were in different cycles, reconnecting them joins the cycles; if they were in one cycle, it splits into two. Every other cycle is unchanged. cards.label: Theorem 10.1
cards.title: What is the equivalence relation \(\sim_L\) modulo \(H\)?
cards.body: An equivalence relation groups elements into disjoint classes by being reflexive, symmetric and transitive. For a subgroup \(H\le G\), define \(a\sim_L b\) when \(a^{-1}b\in H\). Reflexivity follows from \(a^{-1}a=e\in H\). Symmetry follows by taking the inverse: \((a^{-1}b)^{-1}=b^{-1}a\in H\). For transitivity, if \(a^{-1}b,b^{-1}c\in H\), their product \(a^{-1}c\) also lies in \(H\). Its classes are the left cosets of \(H\).

cards.label: Definition 10.2
cards.title: What is a left coset \(aH\)?
cards.body: To form the left coset \(aH\), multiply each \(h\in H\) on the left by a fixed \(a\in G\): \(aH=\{ah:h\in H\}\). It contains \(a=ae\). The element \(a\) is a representative; different representatives can name the same coset. Two left cosets are either equal or disjoint. A coset \(aH\) is a subgroup only when \(a\in H\), in which case it equals \(H\). For additive groups write \(a+H\).
cards.tex: aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}, \qquad a + H = \{a + h \mid h \in H\}

cards.label: Examples 10.3–10.4
cards.title: Left Cosets in \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\) (Examples 10.3–10.4)
cards.body: In Example 10.3, the subgroup \(3\mathbb{Z}\) partitions \(\mathbb{Z}\) into three cosets: \(3\mathbb{Z}\), \(1 + 3\mathbb{Z}\), and \(2 + 3\mathbb{Z}\). Similarly, in Example 10.4, \(H = \langle 3 \rangle = \{0, 3, 6, 9\}\) partitions \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\) into three disjoint cosets of size \(4\).

cards.label: Example 10.5
cards.title: Left Cosets of \(H = \{\iota, \mu\}\) in \(D_4\) (Example 10.5)
cards.body: Here \(D_4\) is the group of eight symmetries of a square: \(\rho\) is rotation by \(90^\circ\), \(\mu\) is reflection, and \(\iota\) is the identity. The rules \(\rho^4=\mu^2=\iota\) and \(\rho\mu=\mu\rho^3\) give \(\rho H=\{\rho,\rho\mu\}=\{\rho,\mu\rho^3\}\). Compute the other cosets the same way. The four displayed pairs account for all eight distinct symmetries.

cards.label: Theorem 10.6
cards.title: Equal Cardinality of Cosets (Theorem 10.6)
cards.body: For fixed \(a\in G\), the map \(f:H\to aH\), \(f(h)=ah\), is a bijection. If \(f(b)=f(c)\), then \(ab=ac\) and cancellation gives \(b=c\), proving one-to-one. Every \(y\in aH\) has the form \(ah\), so \(y=f(h)\), proving onto. Hence \(H\) and \(aH\) have the same cardinality, even if they are infinite. For a finite subgroup, this says every coset has exactly \(|H|\) elements.
cards.tex: f(b) = f(c) \implies ab = ac \implies b = c \text{ (by left cancellation)}

cards.label: Theorem 10.7
cards.title: What is the Theorem of Lagrange?
cards.body: Lagrange’s theorem: if \(G\) is a finite group and \(H\le G\), then \(|H|\) divides \(|G|\). Proof: the left cosets form a partition, so every element of \(G\) is counted exactly once. Each coset has \(|H|\) elements. If there are \(r\) cosets, \(|G|=r|H|\), where \(r\) is an integer. This proves divisibility. The theorem restricts possible subgroup orders; it does not assert that every divisor occurs.
examples: A subgroup of a group of order \(18\) cannot have order \(4\).

cards.label: Corollary 10.8
cards.title: Groups of Prime Order (Corollary 10.8)
cards.body: Corollary 10.8: Every group of prime order \(p\) is cyclic (and isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}_p\)). For \(a \neq e\), \(|\langle a \rangle| = m \ge 2\) divides \(p\) by Lagrange's Theorem, so \(m = p\) and \(G = \langle a \rangle\).
cards.tex: |G| = p \text{ (prime)},\ a \neq e \implies |\langle a \rangle| = p \implies G = \langle a \rangle \simeq \mathbb{Z}_p

cards.label: Theorem 10.9
cards.title: Order of an Element Divides Group Order (Theorem 10.9)
cards.body: Theorem 10.9: The order of an element of a finite group divides the order of the group, because the order of \(a\) equals the order \(|\langle a \rangle|\) of the cyclic subgroup generated by \(a\).

cards.label: Definition 10.10
cards.title: What is the index \((G:H)\) of a subgroup?
cards.body: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a group \(G\). The number of left cosets of \(H\) in \(G\) is the index \((G:H)\) of \(H\) in \(G\). When \(G\) is finite, \((G:H) = |G|/|H|\).

cards.label: Theorem 10.11
cards.title: Multiplicativity of Index (Theorem 10.11 & Exercise 40)
cards.body: If \(K\le H\le G\) and both \([G:H]\) and \([H:K]\) are finite, then \([G:K]=[G:H][H:K]\). This also applies when the groups themselves are infinite. Choose representatives \(a_i\) for the cosets of \(H\) in \(G\), and \(b_j\) for the cosets of \(K\) in \(H\). Every \(g\in G\) has the form \(a_i b_j k\). If \(a_i b_jK=a_u b_vK\), then \(a_iH=a_uH\), so \(i=u\); cancellation then gives \(b_jK=b_vK\), so \(j=v\). The distinct cosets are therefore indexed by all pairs \((i,j)\).

cards.label: Right Cosets
cards.title: What is a right coset \(Ha\)?
cards.body: The relation \(a \sim_R b\) if and only if \(ab^{-1} \in H\) is an equivalence relation on \(G\) whose equivalence classes are the right cosets \(Ha = \{ha \mid h \in H\}\) of \(H\).
cards.tex: Ha = \{ha \mid h \in H\}, \qquad a \sim_R b \iff ab^{-1} \in H

Changing representatives gives the same coset: \(4+5=3\) modulo 6 also lies in \(H\). These three cosets form a group isomorphic to \(\mathbb Z_3\). For a general subgroup this operation may depend on representatives; normality is the condition that makes it well defined.

cards.label: Corollary 10.19
cards.title: One-to-One Homomorphisms via the Kernel (Corollary 10.19 & Example 10.20)
cards.body: A group homomorphism \(\phi:G\to G^{\prime}\) is one-to-one exactly when its kernel is \(\{e\}\). Conversely, if \(\phi\) is one-to-one, \(\phi(x)=e^{\prime}=\phi(e)\) forces \(x=e\). cards.body: For a map \(\phi:X\to Y\), the image \(\phi[A]=\{\phi(a):a\in A\}\) contains the outputs reached from a subset \(A\subseteq X\). cards.title: Definition 8.6: The Kernel of a Homomorphism
cards.body: For a homomorphism \(\phi : G \to G'\), the kernel is \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \phi^{-1}[\{e'\}] = \{x \in G \mid \phi(x) = e'\}\). By Theorem 8.5(4), \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\) is a subgroup of \(G\).

cards.title: Before quotient groups: normal subgroups and coset multiplication
cards.body: A subgroup \(N\le G\) is normal, written \(N\trianglelefteq G\), if \(gN=Ng\) for every \(g\in G\). Equivalently, \(gng^{-1}\in N\) for every \(n\in N,g\in G\). A kernel is normal: \(\phi(gng^{-1})=\phi(g)e^{\prime}\phi(g)^{-1}=e^{\prime}\). For normal \(N\), the quotient (factor) group \(G/N\) has cosets as its elements and operation \((aN)(bN)=(ab)N\). Its identity is the coset \(N\), its inverse of \(aN\) is \(a^{-1}N\), and the canonical homomorphism \(\gamma_N:G\to G/N\) is \(\gamma_N(g)=gN\). A coset is a whole set in \(G\), but one element of \(G/N\).

cards.title: Why normality makes multiplication of cosets well defined
cards.body: An operation on cosets must give the same output however representatives are chosen. Replace \(a\) by \(an_1\) and \(b\) by \(bn_2\), where \(n_1,n_2\in N\). Their product is \((an_1)(bn_2)=ab(b^{-1}n_1b)n_2\). Normality puts \(b^{-1}n_1b\) in \(N\), so the new product still lies in \(abN\). Thus \((aN)(bN)=(ab)N\) is independent of representatives. In an abelian group every subgroup is normal, since \(gn=ng\).

cards.title: Collapsing Cosets into an Isomorphic Image
cards.meaning: The isomorphism theorems explain how collapsing a normal subgroup into the identity element turns a group homomorphism or subgroup lattice into an exact isomorphism of factor groups.

cards.bridge: Theorem 16.2 states this factor-group bridge formally and becomes the main tool used to prove both the Second and Third Isomorphism Theorems.

cards.title: Theorem 16.2 (First Isomorphism Theorem) & Lemma 16.3
cards.body: Let \(\phi:G\to G^{\prime}\) be a homomorphism with kernel \(K\). The First Isomorphism Theorem gives \(G/K\simeq\phi[G]\) via \(\mu(gK)=\phi(g)\). The target is the image, which equals \(G^{\prime}\) only if \(\phi\) is onto. This is the unique map satisfying \(\mu\circ\gamma_K=\phi\), because every coset is \(\gamma_K(g)\). A related correspondence says: for normal \(N\), normal subgroups \(L\) of \(G\) containing \(N\) correspond bijectively to normal subgroups \(L/N\) of \(G/N\), with inverse given by taking the preimage under \(\gamma_N\).

cards.title: Two Linked Operations: Addition and Multiplication
cards.meaning: A ring is a number-like algebraic system with two binary operations, addition and multiplication, where addition forms an abelian group, multiplication is associative, and the distributive laws tie them together.
cards.picture: Axioms R1 (addition) and R2 (multiplication) are connected only through R3 (the distributive laws).
cards.example: The integers Z under usual + and . form our prototype ring; n x n matrices M_n(R) and functions f : R -> R also form rings.
cards.bridge: Definition 22.1 states axioms R1, R2, and R3 formally, and Theorem 22.8 uses R3 to prove that 0a = 0 and (-a)(-b) = ab in every ring.

cards.title: Definition 22.1: Ring
cards.body: A ring has two binary operations, \(+\) and multiplication, both closed on \(R\). Under addition, \(R\) is an abelian group: there is \(0\), each \(a\) has \(-a\), and sums are associative and commutative. Multiplication is associative. The two distributive laws link them: \(a(b+c)=ab+ac\) and \((a+b)c=ac+bc\). Fraleigh’s convention does not require a multiplicative identity, commutative multiplication, or multiplicative inverses. Those are extra properties.
cards.tex: a \cdot (b + c) = (a \cdot b) + (a \cdot c), \quad (a + b) \cdot c = (a \cdot c) + (b \cdot c)

cards.title: Standard ring examples and their operations
cards.body: \(\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q,\mathbb R,\mathbb C\) use usual addition and multiplication. The matrix ring \(M_n(R)\) uses matrix addition and multiplication. The function ring uses pointwise operations, not composition: \((fg)(x)=f(x)g(x)\); all ring laws follow by evaluating at each input and using real arithmetic. The multiples \(n\mathbb Z\) form an additive subgroup closed under multiplication; associativity and distributivity are inherited from \(\mathbb Z\). In \(\mathbb Z_n\), reduce sums and products modulo \(n\). Direct products use each operation component by component. The lines below illustrate these operations; they are not a proof of every ring axiom.

cards.title: Definition 22.9: Ring Homomorphism and Kernel
cards.body: A ring homomorphism \(\phi:R\to R^{\prime}\) must preserve both operations: \(\phi(a+b)=\phi(a)+\phi(b)\) and \(\phi(ab)=\phi(a)\phi(b)\) for all inputs. Its kernel is the set mapped to the additive identity, \(\ker\phi=\{a:\phi(a)=0^{\prime}\}\). Fraleigh does not require \(\phi(1)=1^{\prime}\) as part of this definition. It preserves \(0\) and negatives because it is a homomorphism of additive groups; it is injective exactly when \(\ker\phi=\{0\}\).

cards.title: Example 22.13: Group Isomorphism vs Ring Isomorphism (\(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(2\mathbb{Z}\))
cards.body: Doubling \(\phi:\mathbb Z\to2\mathbb Z\), \(\phi(x)=2x\), is an additive group isomorphism: injectivity, surjectivity and additive preservation were checked in Module I. In fact the rings cannot be isomorphic: \(\mathbb Z\) has unity, and \(2\mathbb Z\) has none; any bijective product-preserving map would carry unity to unity.

cards.body: A subring \(S\subseteq R\) uses the same addition and multiplication and is itself a ring. A practical test is: \(S\ne\varnothing\) and, for every \(a,b\in S\), both \(a-b\in S\) and \(ab\in S\). Taking \(a=b\) supplies 0, and subtraction then supplies negatives and sums; other laws are inherited. cards.title: Definition 23.2: Divisors of 0 (Zero Divisors)
cards.body: A zero divisor is a nonzero element participating in a product \(ab=0\) with another nonzero element. In a noncommutative ring one distinguishes left and right zero divisors; here “zero divisors” includes either side as in Fraleigh. Zero itself is excluded. A unit cannot be a zero divisor: if \(ab=0\), multiply on the left by \(a^{-1}\) to force \(b=0\); if \(ba=0\), multiply on the right. In \(\mathbb Z_{12}\), \(3\cdot4=0\) even though neither factor is zero.

This proof uses no multiplicative inverse. Therefore cancellation in an integral domain implies at most one solution of \(ax=b\), but does not guarantee a solution in the ring: \(2x=1\) has none in \(\mathbb Z\).

cards.title: Integral Domains: Rings Modelled on the Integers Z
cards.meaning: An integral domain is a commutative ring with a nonzero unity and no zero divisors. These are the properties that justify cancelling a nonzero factor and solving a factored equation by setting a factor equal to zero.
cards.picture: In a domain, a product can be zero only when at least one factor is zero. Multiplicative inverses need not exist.
cards.example: In \(\mathbb Z\), \(2x=2y\) implies \(x=y\), but \(2x=1\) has no integer solution. In \(\mathbb Z_{12}\), cancellation fails: \(3\cdot0=3\cdot4=0\).

cards.title: Figure 23.10: Hierarchy of Rings & Exercises 24, 26 (Section 23)
cards.body: Every field is an integral domain: if \(ab=0\) and \(a\ne0\), multiply by \(a^{-1}\) to get \(b=0\). The converse fails for infinite rings: \(\mathbb Z\) is a domain but not a field. Commutativity and existence of unity are independent extra ring properties. For example \(\mathbb Z_6\) has both but has zero divisors; \(2\mathbb Z\) is commutative without unity; \(M_2(\mathbb R)\) has unity but is noncommutative; \(M_2(2\mathbb Z)\) has neither. cards.title: Theorem 23.11: Every Finite Integral Domain is a Field
cards.body: Theorem 23.11: Every finite integral domain is a field. The finiteness condition is necessary because \(\mathbb{Z}\) is an infinite integral domain that is not a field (\(f(x) = 2x\) on \(\mathbb{Z}\) is one-to-one but not onto).
cards.tex: R \text{ finite integral domain} \implies R \text{ is a field}

cards.title: Proof of Theorem 23.11: Counting Argument for Finite Domains
cards.body: Fix arbitrary \(a\ne0\) in a finite integral domain \(R\). Multiplication \(f(x)=ax\) is one-to-one by cancellation. Since there are finitely many inputs and outputs, it is onto, so it hits unity: \(ab=1\) for some \(b\in R\). Commutativity gives \(ba=1\) too. Since every nonzero \(a\) is a unit, \(R\) is a field. Finiteness is essential: on \(\mathbb Z\), \(x\mapsto2x\) is injective but misses 1.

cards.title: Characteristic of a Ring: When Repeated Addition Hits Zero
cards.meaning: The characteristic of a ring is the least positive integer \(n\) such that adding any element \(a\) to itself \(n\) times gives zero. If no single positive integer works for every element, the characteristic is 0.
cards.picture: For a ring with unity, test the repeated sums of 1. In \(\mathbb Z_n\) they first return to 0 after \(n\) additions; in \(\mathbb Z\) they never do.
cards.example: In \(\mathbb Z_6\), \(6\cdot a=0\) for every residue \(a\); smaller positive counts fail for \(a=1\), so its characteristic is 6.
cards.bridge: Definition 23.12 defines characteristic for any ring, and Theorem 23.14 proves that in a ring with unity we only need to check multiples n . 1 of unity 1.

cards.title: Definition 23.12 & Example 23.13: Characteristic of a Ring
cards.body: The characteristic of a ring \(R\) is the least positive integer \(n\) such that \(n \cdot a = 0\) for all \(a \in R\). If no such positive integer exists, \(R\) has characteristic \(0\). Example 23.13: \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb{Z}_n) = n\) and \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb{Z}) = 0\).

cards.title: Theorem 23.14 & Exercise 35 (Section 23): Characteristic via Unity
cards.body: Theorem 23.14: In a ring \(R\) with unity, if \(n \cdot 1 \ne 0\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\), \(\operatorname{char}(R) = 0\); if \(n \cdot 1 = 0\) for some \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\), the smallest such \(n\) is \(\operatorname{char}(R)\). Exercise 35 (Section 23): For a domain \(D\), \(\operatorname{char}(D)\) is \(0\) or prime.

cards.title: Proof of Theorem 23.14: Using Unity \(1\) to Find the Characteristic
cards.body: The proof shows that any positive integer annihilating \(1\) also annihilates every element. Conversely, an integer annihilating every element annihilates \(1\) in particular. Therefore the two sets of possible positive integers agree, so their least elements agree; if neither set has a positive integer, the characteristic is 0.

cards.q: State whether true or false: The characteristic of the ring \(n\mathbb{Z}\) is \(n\) for \(n \ge 1\).
cards.why: By Exercise 23c (Section 23), in \(n\mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}\), no positive integer \(k\) satisfies \(k \cdot a = ka = 0\) for nonzero \(a \in n\mathbb{Z}\), so \(\operatorname{char}(n\mathbb{Z}) = 0\).

cards.why: Theorem 23.11 proves by a counting argument that every finite integral domain is a field.

cards.q: Find the characteristic of the ring \(\mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_4\) (Exercise 9 (Section 23)).
cards.why: By Theorem 23.14, we seek the smallest \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\) with \(n \cdot (1, 1) = (0, 0)\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_4\), which is \(\operatorname{lcm}(3, 4) = 12\).
